questions.title: Impaired defence turns normal flora into opportunistic pathogens
questions.question: Normal flora cause infection when body defense is impaired is called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A saprophyte lives on dead or decaying organic matter in the environment, not on or in a living host, so the term does not describe a normal-flora organism turning pathogenic in an immunocompromised patient.
explanations.B: Correct. Members of a person's own normal flora ordinarily coexist harmlessly with the host, but they can cause disease specifically when host defences are compromised, as in immunocompromised patients. This condition-dependent behaviour is exactly what defines an opportunistic pathogen, distinguishing it from a true (obligate) pathogen that frequently causes disease even in healthy subjects.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Endo-parasite" describes a parasite living inside the host's body, a parasitology term, not the standard microbiology term for a normal-flora organism that becomes pathogenic under compromised host defences.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A true (obligate) pathogen typically causes disease in healthy subjects as its usual behaviour, unlike an opportunistic organism, which specifically requires a compromised host to become clinically significant.

questions.learning_objective: State that a normal-flora organism causing disease specifically when host defences are impaired is termed an opportunistic pathogen.

questions.title: Bacteria have no mitochondria
questions.question: Bacterial cell does not contain?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bacteria (with rare exceptions such as Mycoplasma) do have a cell wall, the structure giving the cell its shape and rigidity.
explanations.B: Correct. Bacteria are prokaryotes and lack membrane-bound organelles entirely, including mitochondria. Where a eukaryotic cell houses its respiratory-chain enzymes in mitochondria, a bacterial cell instead carries out respiration at its cytoplasmic membrane, classically at membrane invaginations called mesosomes. This absence of mitochondria is a defining structural difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bacteria do contain 70S ribosomes, the smaller ribosome size characteristic of prokaryotes, distinct from the 80S ribosomes of eukaryotic cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mesosomes are cytoplasmic membrane invaginations found in bacteria, classically described as housing respiratory enzymes and coordinating chromosome segregation.

questions.learning_objective: State that bacteria lack mitochondria, while correctly possessing a cell wall, 70S ribosomes and mesosomes.

questions.title: Spore coat and cortex confer resistance to drying and heat
questions.question: Resistance of spores to drying and heat is due to?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Spores are characteristically dehydrated, with a markedly lower water content than a vegetative cell, not a higher one -- this dehydration itself is part of what confers resistance, the reverse of this option's claim.
explanations.B: Correct. The spore's dense, multilayered coat and underlying cortex form a highly impermeable barrier around the dehydrated core, physically restricting the penetration of water, heat and chemical disinfectants. This structural barrier, together with the core's own dehydration and its calcium-dipicolinate-stabilised DNA, is a standard, testable explanation for a spore's exceptional resistance to drying and heat.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A spore is metabolically dormant, not highly active -- this near-total metabolic shutdown is itself part of the survival strategy, not a source of heat resistance.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A spore does not multiply at all; it is a dormant, non-replicating survival stage that must first germinate back into a vegetative cell before any multiplication can resume.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Spore resistance is associated with a high, not low, content of calcium dipicolinate, which complexes with core DNA and helps stabilise it against heat damage -- this option reverses the actual relationship.

questions.learning_objective: State that the spore coat and cortex confer resistance to drying and heat, while rejecting higher water content, metabolic activity, multiplication and low calcium dipicolinate as the mechanism.

questions.title: Bacteriocin production is plasmid-encoded
questions.question: Genetic information about bacteriocin production in bacteria is a function of?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ribosomes carry out protein synthesis; they do not carry the genetic information determining which proteins, such as bacteriocins, a cell is capable of producing.
explanations.B: Correct. Bacteriocin production -- the ability of a bacterium to synthesise a protein toxin that kills competing bacterial strains -- is a classic example of a plasmid-encoded, accessory trait. As with antibiotic resistance and virulence genes, the genetic information for bacteriocin production is typically carried on a plasmid rather than the core chromosome, making it a dispensable, transmissible property.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mesosomes are cytoplasmic membrane invaginations with a structural and respiratory role, not a genetic-information-carrying structure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The chromosome carries the genes essential for the bacterium's core, universal cellular life, not typically the accessory, strain-variable trait of bacteriocin production.

questions.learning_objective: State that bacteriocin production is genetically encoded on a plasmid, not the ribosomes, mesosomes or chromosome.

questions.title: Plasmids are dispensable, not essential, genetic elements
questions.question: Plasmids are?

options.D: Carry genetic material essential for bacterial life

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cytoplasmic storage (inclusion) granules are reserve-nutrient structures such as volutin or glycogen granules, a wholly different structure from a plasmid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A plasmid is a DNA molecule, not RNA -- it is a small, circular, double-stranded DNA element separate from the chromosome.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A plasmid is extrachromosomal DNA by definition, distinct from the bacterium's own chromosomal DNA.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is specifically the chromosome that carries the genetic material essential for the bacterium's core life processes -- a plasmid instead carries accessory, non-essential genes.
explanations.E: Correct. A plasmid typically carries accessory genes, such as antibiotic-resistance or virulence genes, that are advantageous but not required for the cell's basic survival. Because these genes are not essential, plasmids are properly described as dispensable genetic elements: a bacterium can lose a plasmid and still survive, unlike loss of its chromosome.

questions.learning_objective: State that plasmids are dispensable, non-essential DNA elements, rejecting storage-granule, RNA, chromosomal-DNA and essential-gene descriptions.

questions.title: Spores protect bacteria against unfavourable conditions
questions.question: Protect bacteria from unfavorable environmental conditions?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cell wall gives the bacterium its shape and rigidity and is a site of action for some antibiotics; it is not the structure formed specifically as a survival response to adverse conditions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The capsule's defining role is antiphagocytic protection and organism identification, not survival of drying, heat or nutrient depletion.
explanations.C: Correct. Certain Gram-positive genera, classically Bacillus and Clostridium, form a highly resistant, metabolically dormant endospore in response to nutrient limitation and other unfavourable environmental conditions. This spore can survive drying, heat and disinfectants far better than the ordinary vegetative cell, then germinate back into an active cell once conditions become favourable again.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The flagellum is the organelle of motility, propelling the cell through liquid; it plays no role in surviving unfavourable environmental conditions.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the spore as the structure protecting bacteria from unfavourable environmental conditions, distinct from the cell wall, capsule and flagella.

questions.title: Spores can vegetate again once conditions favour germination
questions.question: Which of the following statement regarding bacterial spores is false?

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement, not the false one). A spore is genuinely metabolically dormant, its enzymatic and biosynthetic activity almost entirely shut down until germination.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement, not the false one). A dormant spore does not multiply; only after it germinates back into a vegetative cell can replication resume.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the false statement. A spore is not permanently locked in its dormant form -- once environmental conditions become favourable again (moisture, nutrients, warmth), it germinates, re-hydrates and returns to an actively growing, dividing vegetative cell. "Unable to vegetate again" misstates this defining, reversible feature of the spore life cycle.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement, not the false one). Spores are markedly resistant to disinfectants and to boiling, a resistance that ordinary vegetative cells lack.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that a spore's inability to vegetate again is the false statement, since spores do germinate back into vegetative cells under favourable conditions.

questions.title: Volutin granules store polyphosphate
questions.question: Volutin granules are?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Volutin granules are not a carbohydrate storage form -- glycogen is the classic bacterial carbohydrate storage granule, a distinct structure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Volutin granules are not composed of protein; they are a phosphate-storage structure, not a protein-storage one.
explanations.C: Correct. Volutin granules, also called metachromatic or Babes-Ernst granules, are cytoplasmic inclusion (storage) granules composed largely of stored polyphosphate. They stain a different colour from the surrounding cytoplasm with certain dyes, such as methylene blue -- a long-standing microscopic aid to organism identification, classically demonstrated in Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Since polyphosphate correctly describes volutin granules, "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Identify volutin (metachromatic) granules as a polyphosphate storage structure, rejecting carbohydrate and protein descriptions.

questions.title: The cytoplasmic membrane is not polysaccharide in nature
questions.question: The following statement are true regarding cytoplasmic membrane EXCEPT?

options.D: Play a role in toxins excretion

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement, not the EXCEPT). The cytoplasmic membrane lies immediately beneath the cell wall, external to it in the layered bacterial envelope.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. The cytoplasmic membrane is a phospholipid bilayer, not a polysaccharide structure -- polysaccharide is instead characteristic of capsular material or the LPS component of a Gram-negative outer membrane, not the cytoplasmic membrane itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement, not the EXCEPT). The cytoplasmic membrane, once stripped of the protective cell wall, is genuinely osmotically sensitive and can rupture under osmotic stress (as demonstrated by protoplast/spheroplast fragility).
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement, not the EXCEPT). The cytoplasmic membrane, alongside the periplasmic space in Gram-negative bacteria, is involved in the excretion of toxins and other extracellular enzymes.
explanations.E: Incorrect (true statement, not the EXCEPT). The cytoplasmic membrane houses the respiratory-chain enzymes that substitute for the mitochondrion a bacterium lacks, classically at membrane invaginations called mesosomes.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that the cytoplasmic membrane is not polysaccharide in nature, while correctly locating it beneath the cell wall and recognising its roles in osmotic sensitivity, toxin excretion and respiration.

questions.title: The cytoplasmic membrane is a phospholipid bilayer
questions.question: Phospholipid bilayer?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cell wall's structural mesh is peptidoglycan (plus, in Gram-negative bacteria, an outer LPS-containing membrane) -- a phospholipid bilayer describes the membrane beneath it, not the wall itself.
explanations.B: Correct. The bacterial cytoplasmic (plasma) membrane is a phospholipid bilayer, the same basic lipid-bilayer architecture found in eukaryotic cell membranes. It sits immediately beneath the cell wall and forms the selectively permeable barrier controlling what enters and leaves the cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The capsule is a polysaccharide (or, in Bacillus anthracis, polypeptide) outer layer, not a phospholipid bilayer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A spore is a dormant, dehydrated survival structure with a dense protective coat and cortex, not defined by a phospholipid bilayer architecture.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the cytoplasmic membrane as the phospholipid bilayer structure, distinct from the cell wall, capsule and spore.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Plasmids do not control basic cell multiplication
questions.question: Plasmids control the following processes in bacteria EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Basic cell multiplication (binary fission) is a core, chromosome-directed process the cell performs regardless of which plasmids it carries -- a plasmid can be replicated and partitioned alongside cell division, but it does not itself control whether or how the cell multiplies.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement, not the EXCEPT). Antibiotic-resistance genes are a classic example of plasmid-encoded, accessory traits.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement, not the EXCEPT). Virulence genes, such as those encoding adhesins or invasion factors, are frequently plasmid-encoded.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement, not the EXCEPT). Many bacterial exotoxins, such as diphtheria toxin (phage-encoded) and several enterotoxins, are encoded on plasmids or other mobile genetic elements rather than the core chromosome.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that basic cell multiplication, not antibiotic resistance, virulence or toxin production, is the process a plasmid does not control.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Selective permeability is a cytoplasmic membrane function
questions.question: Selective permeability is a function of?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cell wall gives the bacterium its shape and rigidity and is generally freely permeable to small solutes, not the selectively permeable barrier controlling molecular traffic.
explanations.B: Correct. The cytoplasmic membrane is the cell's selectively permeable barrier, regulating which materials pass into and out of the cell. This is a direct consequence of its phospholipid bilayer architecture, which restricts free diffusion of most molecules and requires transport proteins for controlled passage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The capsule's defining role is antiphagocytic protection and organism identification, not regulating molecular traffic into and out of the cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A spore is a dormant survival structure with a dense, impermeable coat designed to exclude water and chemicals almost entirely, not to provide the cell's ordinary selective-permeability function.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the cytoplasmic membrane as the structure responsible for selective permeability, distinct from the cell wall, capsule and spore.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Inclusion granules are reserved nutrients
questions.question: Inclusion granules?

options.B: Present only in gram negative bacilli

explanations.A: Incorrect. Inclusion granules appear and disappear depending on nutrient availability; they are not a fixed, permanent structure present in every cell at all times.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Inclusion granules occur across a range of bacteria, not restricted to Gram-negative bacilli -- Corynebacterium diphtheriae, a Gram-positive rod, is a classic example bearing prominent inclusion granules.
explanations.C: Correct. Inclusion (storage) granules -- such as volutin/metachromatic (polyphosphate), glycogen (carbohydrate) or poly-beta-hydroxybutyrate (lipid) granules -- are cytoplasmic reserves of nutrients. The cell accumulates them when a given nutrient is abundant and draws on them when conditions later become limiting. This storage-and-mobilisation pattern is what "reserved nutrients" describes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inclusion granules are typically composed of polyphosphate, carbohydrate or lipid, not protein.

questions.learning_objective: State that inclusion granules are reserved-nutrient storage structures, not permanent, Gram-negative-restricted or protein in nature.

questions.title: Capsule, pili, exotoxins and Lipid A are all virulence factors
questions.question: Bacterial structure that may be associated with pathogenicity are the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement, but incomplete). The capsule is genuinely a virulence factor, chiefly through its antiphagocytic action, but it is only one of several listed here.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement, but incomplete). Pili contribute to pathogenicity through adherence to host cells, but this too is only part of the full picture.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement, but incomplete). Exotoxins are secreted virulence factors that directly damage host cells or disrupt their function, again only one of several correct options here.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement, but incomplete). Lipid A, the toxic component of Gram-negative lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin), triggers inflammatory and septic effects, but this alone does not capture the full list.
explanations.E: Correct. Capsule, pili, exotoxins and Lipid A are all genuine, well-established bacterial virulence factors, each contributing to pathogenicity through a different mechanism -- antiphagocytic protection, adherence, direct cell damage and endotoxic activity respectively. Since all four are correct, "all of the above" is the accurate answer.

questions.learning_objective: State that the capsule, pili, exotoxins and Lipid A are all bacterial structures/products associated with pathogenicity.

questions.title: Both penicillin and lysozyme can produce protoplasts
questions.question: Protoplasts are developed due to effect of?

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement, but incomplete). Penicillin, by inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking during wall synthesis, can lead to a wall-deficient protoplast in a Gram-positive cell, but it is not the only agent capable of this.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement, but incomplete). Lysozyme, by directly hydrolysing existing peptidoglycan, can likewise strip a Gram-positive cell of its wall to leave a protoplast, but again this is not the sole correct option.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Polyenes (such as amphotericin B) act on ergosterol in fungal cell membranes; they are not the classic agents used to produce a bacterial protoplast.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Polymyxins disrupt the bacterial outer/cytoplasmic membrane directly; they are not the classic wall-removing agents that generate a protoplast.
explanations.E: Correct. A Gram-positive bacterium's protoplast is a cell stripped entirely of its peptidoglycan wall. Either penicillin, which blocks new wall synthesis, or lysozyme, which hydrolyses existing wall material, can produce it, since both routes remove the peptidoglycan a Gram-positive cell relies on. What remains after either treatment is only the fragile, osmotically sensitive cytoplasmic membrane.

questions.learning_objective: State that both penicillin and lysozyme can each produce a protoplast from a Gram-positive bacterium.

questions.title: Antibiotic-destroying enzymes are excreted at the cytoplasmic membrane
questions.question: The following is site of excretion of enzymes that destroy antibiotics?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The capsule's role is antiphagocytic protection, not the site through which antibiotic-inactivating enzymes leave the cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cell wall (specifically its peptidoglycan) is itself a common antibiotic target, not the excretion route for the enzymes that inactivate antibiotics.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Spores are dormant survival structures, unrelated to enzyme excretion or antibiotic resistance mechanisms of an actively growing cell.
explanations.D: Correct. Bacteria that inactivate antibiotics enzymatically -- classically beta-lactamases hydrolysing the beta-lactam ring of penicillins and cephalosporins -- excrete these enzymes at or through the cytoplasmic membrane. In a Gram-negative cell this means release into the periplasmic space; in a Gram-positive cell it means release directly into the surrounding medium. Either way, the cytoplasmic membrane is the shared excretion route.

questions.learning_objective: State that antibiotic-inactivating enzymes are excreted at the cytoplasmic membrane, not the capsule, cell wall or spore.

questions.title: Curved rod-shaped bacteria are vibrios
questions.question: Bacteria shaped like curved rods?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cocci are spherical bacteria, not curved rods.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bacilli are straight rod-shaped bacteria; a curved rod is a distinct morphological category from a straight one.
explanations.C: Correct. Bacteria shaped like curved or comma-shaped rods are classified as vibrios. Vibrio cholerae, the cause of cholera, is the classic example of this morphology, its single polar flagellum driving a characteristic rapid, darting motility.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Spirochaetes are long, thin, flexible, helically coiled organisms, a more extensively coiled shape than a vibrio's simple curve.

questions.learning_objective: Identify vibrios as the curved, comma-shaped rod bacterial morphology, distinguishing it from cocci, bacilli and spirochaetes.

questions.title: The bacterial chromosome controls cell properties and behaviour
questions.question: Function of bacterial chromosome is?

options.D: Used as vector for gene cloning

explanations.A: Correct. The bacterial chromosome -- a single, circular, double-stranded DNA molecule held free in the cytoplasm's nucleoid region -- carries the genetic information that controls the cell's inherited properties and behaviour: its structural features, metabolic capabilities and environmental responses. This genome-level control function is the chromosome's defining role.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Protein synthesis is physically carried out by ribosomes reading messenger RNA, not by the chromosome itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Respiratory enzymes are housed at the cytoplasmic membrane, classically at mesosomes, not on the chromosome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Small, easily manipulated plasmids -- not the much larger chromosome -- are the classic vectors used in gene cloning.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Since protein synthesis, respiration and cloning-vector use are each carried out by other cell components (ribosomes, the membrane, plasmids), "all of the above" incorrectly attributes them to the chromosome as well.

questions.learning_objective: State that the bacterial chromosome's function is to control the cell's genetically determined properties and behaviour, rejecting protein synthesis, respiration and cloning-vector use.

questions.title: Failure to retain crystal violet after decolorization defines Gram-negative bacteria
questions.question: Bacteria whose cell can't retain methyl violet after decolorization with alcohol are?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acid-fastness is a separate staining property (resistance to acid-alcohol decolorization after carbol fuchsin, classically in Mycobacterium), not the Gram stain's own decolorization behaviour.
explanations.B: Correct. Gram-negative bacteria have only a thin peptidoglycan layer, which the alcohol decolourising step readily disrupts, washing out the crystal violet-iodine complex (loosely termed "methyl violet" here). Because the primary stain is lost at decolorization, the cell instead takes up the safranin counterstain and appears pink, the defining Gram-negative result.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall that retains the crystal violet-iodine complex through the decolourising step -- the opposite of the behaviour this question describes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Anaerobic/aerobic growth requirement is an unrelated property to Gram-stain decolorization behaviour.

questions.learning_objective: State that failure to retain the primary Gram stain after alcohol decolorization defines Gram-negative bacteria.

questions.title: Restriction enzymes are not required for chromosomal replication
questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding bacterial cell division?

options.B: Restriction enzymes is required for chromosomal replication
options.C: Mesosomes play a role in cell division
options.D: The cell divided into two daughter identical cells

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement, not the incorrect one). Bacteria do multiply by binary fission, the simple splitting of one cell into two.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the incorrect statement being asked for. Restriction endonucleases recognise a specific DNA sequence and cleave it, classically as part of a phage-defence system, but they play no role in the routine replication of the bacterium's own chromosome -- so they are not required for chromosomal replication, contrary to this statement.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement, not the incorrect one). Mesosomes have classically been described as anchoring the bacterial chromosome and coordinating its segregation during cell division.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement, not the incorrect one). Binary fission produces two genetically identical daughter cells, the standard outcome of bacterial cell division.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that restriction enzymes are not required for chromosomal replication, while correctly recognising binary fission, mesosome involvement and identical daughter cells as true statements about bacterial cell division.

questions.title: Spores form in Gram-positive, not Gram-negative, cells
questions.question: All the following statements refer to bacterial spores EXCEPT?

options.A: They are formed within certain gram-negative cells
options.B: They do not take ordinary stains
options.D: They are more resistant than vegetative cells

explanations.A: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Endospore formation (sporulation) is classically a Gram-positive property, seen in genera such as Bacillus and Clostridium -- not a Gram-negative one, contrary to this statement.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement, not the EXCEPT). The dense, resistant spore coat does not take up ordinary stains, appearing as unstained, clear/refractile areas on a routine smear.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement, not the EXCEPT). Spores are genuinely dehydrated, with markedly lower water content than a vegetative cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement, not the EXCEPT). Spores are far more resistant to heat, drying and disinfectants than the vegetative cells that form them.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that spore formation is a Gram-positive, not a Gram-negative, property, while correctly recognising staining, dehydration and resistance features.

questions.title: The nucleoid lacks a nuclear membrane
questions.question: Bacterial nucleoid differs from eukaryotic nucleus in being?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bacterial DNA is not organised around histone proteins the way eukaryotic chromatin is -- the nucleoid lacks true histones, so this is not a feature distinguishing it from a eukaryotic nucleus in the direction implied here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ribosomes are found free in the cytoplasm surrounding the nucleoid, not inside it, in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells' respective compartments; this is not the defining structural difference asked for.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The bacterial nucleoid typically holds a single circular chromosome, not multiple ones -- multiple linear chromosomes are the eukaryotic pattern, the reverse of this option's claim.
explanations.D: Correct. The bacterial nucleoid is an unbound region of cytoplasm holding the cell's DNA, with no membrane enclosing it -- unlike the eukaryotic nucleus, whose DNA is enclosed within a double nuclear membrane. This absence of a nuclear membrane is the defining structural distinction between the two.

questions.learning_objective: State that the bacterial nucleoid, unlike the eukaryotic nucleus, lacks a nuclear membrane.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Crystal violet stains Gram-positive bacteria
questions.question: Staining material of gram-positive bacterium is?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fast green is a histology counterstain used in some tissue-staining protocols, not the Gram stain's primary reagent.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hematoxylin is a histology nuclear stain (as in H&E staining), not a Gram stain reagent.
explanations.C: Correct. Crystal violet is the Gram stain's primary dye. A Gram-positive bacterium's thick peptidoglycan wall retains the crystal violet-iodine complex through the alcohol decolourising step. This retention is what produces the characteristic violet/purple appearance defining a Gram-positive result.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Safranin is the Gram stain's counterstain, taken up specifically by Gram-negative cells after they lose the primary crystal violet stain -- it is not what a Gram-positive cell retains.

questions.learning_objective: Identify crystal violet as the dye retained by, and defining, a Gram-positive bacterium on Gram stain.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Lysozyme hydrolyzes the bacterial cell wall
questions.question: Enzyme hydrolyzing bacterial cell wall?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A lysosome is a eukaryotic membrane-bound organelle containing digestive enzymes, not itself an enzyme, and not a bacterial structure at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A reductase catalyses reduction reactions in metabolic pathways; it does not hydrolyse peptidoglycan.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A protease breaks down proteins; peptidoglycan is a sugar-peptide polymer whose glycosidic bonds are not a protease's substrate.
explanations.D: Correct. Lysozyme hydrolyses the beta-1,4 glycosidic bond between the alternating sugar units of peptidoglycan, breaking down the bacterial cell wall. Applied to a Gram-positive cell, this can strip the wall away entirely, leaving a wall-deficient protoplast.

questions.learning_objective: Identify lysozyme as the enzyme that hydrolyses the bacterial cell wall.

questions.title: Corynebacterium diphtheriae causes diphtheria
questions.question: Diphtheria is caused by?

explanations.A: Correct. Diphtheria, an upper-respiratory-tract infection classically marked by a grey pseudomembrane and toxin-mediated complications such as myocarditis, is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, a Gram-positive, club-shaped rod. The same organism is also classically recognised microscopically by its prominent cytoplasmic metachromatic (Babes-Ernst) storage granules.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Staphylococcus species cause a different spectrum of disease (skin/soft-tissue infections, toxic shock, food poisoning), not diphtheria.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Streptococcus species cause a different spectrum of disease (pharyngitis, rheumatic fever, necrotising fasciitis among others), not diphtheria.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Since Corynebacterium correctly names diphtheria's causative organism, "none of these" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Corynebacterium diphtheriae as the causative organism of diphtheria, distinguishing it from Staphylococcus and Streptococcus.

questions.title: Treponema pallidum is the classic spirochete
questions.question: Spirochete is?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gonococci (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) are Gram-negative diplococci, a spherical, paired morphology, not a spirochete.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Staphylococci are Gram-positive cocci arranged in clusters, not a spirochete.
explanations.C: Correct. Treponema pallidum, the cause of syphilis, is the classic clinically relevant spirochete. It is a long, thin, flexible, helically coiled organism, motile by internal axial filaments rather than external flagella. This shape and motility pattern is distinct from the spherical cocci listed among the other options.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Streptococci are Gram-positive cocci arranged in chains, not a spirochete.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Treponema pallidum as the classic spirochete, distinguishing it from the coccal genera Neisseria, Staphylococcus and Streptococcus.
